newsitem.title: FRANCE: IHT staff protest at Scientology advertising.
newsitem.headline: IHT staff protest at Scientology advertising.

text.p: Members of the International Herald Tribune staff bought space in their own newspaper on Saturday to protest at an advertising campaign by the Church of Scientology and say it did not reflect the daily's values.
In a brief ad, the protesters said: "An advertisement is not a reflection of the moral and editorial values of a newspaper".
They added that they wanted "to emphasise their moral disagreement with the Scientology advertisement placed in yesterday's newspaper".

The seven-line note, paid for by members of the newspaper's staff in Paris, Frankfurt and Zurich, followed a Scientology advertisement of announcing over three quarters of a page the launch of an information campaign for the church.
The U.S.-based church said in a statement on Saturday its advertising campaign in the International Herald Tribune and the British weekly The Economist would go on for months.
It would be the group's biggest information campaign ever in order to "tell the Scientology's true story".
Scientology was founded in 1954 by the American science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard, who said he had discovered Dianetics, or the science of mental health.

Twenty-three members of the church's French branch went on trial in the central city of Lyon earlier this month on charges ranging from embezzlement to manslaughter following the 1988 suicide of church member Patrice Vic.
The prosecution requested fines and suspended prison sentences, saying Vic threw himself to his death from a high-rise block because he could not raise the cash to go on a Scientology course.
The court will announce its verdict on November 22.
Scientology has also come into trouble in Germany where Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) pledged to put it under official surveillance and bar its members from public service.
The group bought a full page in the New York Times last Thursday to accuse Germany, in an ad showing the eagle and swastika insignia of Hitler's Third Reich, of Nazi persecution.
Germany replied that the charges were absurd and an insult to millions of Jewish victims of the Holocaust.
